source.title: Get rich quick: exact solutions reveal how unbalanced initializations promote rapid feature learning
source.authors: D. Kunin; Allan Ravent'os; C. Dominé; Feng Chen; D. Klindt; Andrew M. Saxe; Surya Ganguli

record.tranche_reason: The paper studies initialization balance and rich versus lazy feature learning, not the listed versions about training classification error, bad local minima, depth and shortcuts, activation-matched initialization trainability, learning-rate stability, or batch normalization.
record.gate_note: The study reports results on its own feature-learning and generalization questions. Its classification accuracies, training loss, and grokking results do not test the behavior specified by these claim versions. Figure-only values and cited prior-work results are not extracted as rows.
record.test_reason: The study measures how relative layer initialization affects feature learning, generalization and task performance. It does not test activation-matched signal or gradient preservation in V4, width-dependent spurious minima in V2, or the training behaviors specified by the other versions. Initialization-dependent feature learning and transformer training speed alone do not establish V4.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. Initialization scale, layer balance and layer-specific learning rates determine lazy versus rich dynamics; balanced initialization enables rapid rich learning in linear networks, while upstream imbalance can accelerate it in nonlinear networks. Extending the theory to deeper nonlinear networks and incorporating discrete, stochastic optimization remain limitations.
record.recipe_differences: The paper investigates gradient-flow dynamics, initialization balance, NTK evolution, activation changes, and task performance. The listed versions concern different optimization and architecture claims; its CNN experiments use SGD but do not test those claims.
record.method_sensitivity: The study reports effects varying with overall scale, relative scale, and initialization manipulation across its own feature-learning experiments; these are outside the listed versions.

fits_no_version.finding: Relative initialization scale changes kernel evolution, activation patterns and feature alignment; upstream initialization accelerates rich learning in the nonlinear settings.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Layer balance at initialization controls the speed and extent of feature learning in the tested networks.

fits_no_version.finding: Initialization manipulations change CNN filter smoothness, hierarchical-task sample complexity and modular-arithmetic grokking time.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Relative initialization scale affects learned representations and generalization in the tested tasks.

fits_no_version.finding: Figure 12 also measures steps to 99% training accuracy across embedding initialization and output scales in a one-layer transformer.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Initialization and output scaling affect time to a training-accuracy threshold in the tested modular-arithmetic transformer.

record.problems: The conclusion notes that the theory does not extend readily to deeper nonlinear networks and omits discretization and stochastic SGD effects. Some empirical outcomes are shown only in figures; the supplied text describes averages over runs for some experiments but does not provide uncertainty estimates for the reported curves.
record.rows_left_out: No rows meet the requirement of directly measuring a behavior named by V1–V6. The paper's experiment results concern related but distinct feature-learning and task-performance outcomes; no qualifying rows were extracted.

untested.parts: Near-zero CIFAR training classification error in sufficiently large networks, including corrupted labels, and its dependence on size, training duration and regularization. Figure 11 reports comparable CIFAR-10 accuracies across initialization scales without establishing this effect.

Spurious-minimum frequency as teacher and student widths grow together, and its reduction with one or two extra student neurons. The teacher-student experiments fix a wide student and vary initialization.
Training degradation with depth and its prevention by identity shortcuts or special initialization recipes.
Activation-matched initialization preserving signals and gradients, resulting training speed and trainable depth, and orthogonal versus Gaussian initialization.
Loss recovery, curvature evolution and divergence relative to a measured learning-rate stability threshold.
Training speed and learning-rate tolerance with versus without batch normalization, including the Fixup comparison.

record.verdict_notes: The record's relation should change from tests to discusses; T6 and the empty result rows are appropriate. Figure 10's near-zero regression loss does not measure CIFAR classification error or width-dependent spurious-minimum frequency. He initialization is used as an experimental starting point, without testing its signal-preservation or depth benefits.

versions.untested_parts: Training classification error from random initialization on CIFAR benchmarks, corrupted or random labels, and effects of model size, training duration, early stopping, and regularization.
Spurious-minimum frequency in two-layer ReLU teacher-student problems as teacher and student width change.
Depth-related training error in plain versus residual convolutional networks, and deep plain or unnormalized residual networks.
Activation-matched initialization, signal or gradient propagation, training speed by initialization, and trainable depth in plain networks.
Training outcomes and curvature behavior at learning rates above or near stability limits.
Batch normalization's effects on accuracy speed and learning-rate tolerance, and Fixup's normalization-free comparison.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
